newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australian Grain-Harvest underway, rain looms.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australian Grain-Harvest underway, rain looms.

text.p: Australia's wheat harvest is underway this week as a pensive mood overhangs grains markets.

After watching wheat prices fall about 40 percent since April, growers in northern New South Wales (NSW) and southern Queensland are harvesting with recent rain having fallen and with forecast rain threatening.

A wet harvest would add further downward price pressure through part of the new crop being turned to feed wheat. Already part of the central Queensland crop has been downgraded by rain. "Rain is at the forefront of every producer's concern with the
threat of feed wheat," said Guy Allen of GrainCorp. "We would expect to see some deliveries (from harvest) late next week from the far north areas," he said.
Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders, a unit of the Geneva-based Romak trading group, said the prospect of a wet harvest weighed on the market.
"It's not a good sign. Harvesting has stopped around Moree because it's raining. You wouldn't want it to continue."
"(A wet harvest) would be a pretty ugly scenario given the amount of feed wheat in Canada," he said.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) is expected to underline the wheat market slide by announcing a cut in its 1996/97 pool price on Monday evening, from the existing benchmark of A$195.00 a tonne for Australian Standard White (ASW).

Allen said the trade expected a price cut of A$5.00-A$10.00. The looming pool price revision was the main overhanging feature of last week's market as everyone watchet U.S. export markets continue to work their way lower, he said. Some farmer hedge selling emerged Friday ahead of the pool revision.
Allen saw ASW's cash price fall by about A$4.00 to A$150.00-A$152.00 over the past week, with the milling wheat price also down about A$4.00 over the week.
Sorghum also edged back to A$160.00-A$165.00 Newcastle.
The barley market was very choppy and mixed, Allen said, with bids ending last week at $125.00-A$130.00 in NSW feedlots. Prices in upcountry silos were A$105.00-A$110.00.
Howard reported a "massive slide" in barley prices over the week in reaction to weak international demand and an absence of buying by feedlots. "It's a very ugly market," he said.
"Our guys are certainly very bearish," he said of wheat.

There were few cash prices in the wheat market in the past week because of lack of activity, he said. With pool prices well above cash prices, trade from farmers was limited, he said. "Everyone's holding back waiting to see (if) cash prices improve," he said. Covering may emerge during harvest.
The AWB's indicative price for new crop ASW wheat delivered Newcastle fell A$4.00 a tonne to A$151.00 over the week.
Australian wheat futures fell over the week in both near-term and in the more distant contracts.
Settlement prices of market leader January 1997 fell to A$154.00 on Friday from A$156.50 on Monday.
Medium-term contracts were mostly steady but January 1998 fell to A$144.50 from A$165.00, with November 1997 and March 1998 strongly down.

A moderately-active week on the SFE saw 89 futures contracts change hands, ahead of the 14 A$150.00 January 1997 put options which traded at A$5.50, creating a worst-case price of A$144.50. AWB Indicative Cash Prices for Oct 18, new crop A$/tonne
Fremantle Adelaide Melbourne Newcastle Brisbane
Note: Australian Standard White = ASW; Australian Hard = AH
